title: SoftBank Credit Insurance Costs Hit 4 Year High on AI Investment Risks

tickers.name: Arm Holdings plc American Depositary Shares

summary:
The cost of protecting against a default on SoftBank's debt climbed to its highest level since 2022 as the market reacted to OpenAI postponing its initial public offering until 2027. The surge in credit risk costs coincided with a fresh 10.8% decline in SoftBank's shares on Friday, adding to a slide that has eroded 59% of the company's value since early June. The Japanese investor has borrowed at record yields to finance its $64.6B stake in OpenAI and other artificial intelligence ventures.

Concerns are also mounting over SB Energy, a SoftBank data center builder that projected $439B in contracted revenue in an IPO filing despite not yet operating any facilities. Market analysts warn that recent midterm election results could lead Democratic governors in key U.S. states to slow development at planned sites, potentially affecting one-third of the country's projected data center capacity for 2027-2028. These pressures follow a 51% drop in the price of Arm shares since June 30, though SoftBank's reported leverage of 13% remains below its internal 25% limit.

SOFTBANK PLUNGES 59% AS DEBT-FUELED AI BETS UNRAVEL

SoftBank shares fell another 10.8% Friday, extending losses to 59% since early June.

The company added $40.4 billion in debt over 12 months to fund AI investments, including $64 billion in OpenAI.

Meanwhile, Arm shares have plunged 51% since June 30, weakening SoftBank's asset backing as credit-default swaps rise and bond prices fall.

SoftBank's reported leverage was 13%, below its self-imposed 25% limit, suggesting a substantial remaining cushion.

SoftBank trades as a proxy for AI spending through its $64.6B OpenAI stake, 90% of Arm and data-centre builder SB Energy.

And its shares fell 10.8% on Friday as the cost of insuring its debt (credit risk) hit a 4-year high.

It has borrowed at record yields to fund the OpenAI stake, while OpenAI’s IPO delay to 2027 pushes back any return.

SB Energy’s IPO filing projects $439B in contracted revenue, yet it operates no data centres and depends heavily on OpenAI.

After midterm wins, democratic  governors in states hosting planned sites may slow development.

And one-third of planned 2027-2028 US data-centre capacity are in those states, though most 2027 projects already secured power and chips.
